archetype.name: Fringe Contender (defense-first)
archetype.definition: Denver has a top-ten defense for the third straight season, and it is propping up a bottom-ten offense and a 3-0 record in one-score games, so the team sits closer to average than its 3-2 suggests.

report.headline: A real defense and three coin-flip wins are covering for a stalled offense.
report.take:
This is Sean Payton's third season with the same formula. The defense is the identity. It ranked 1st in EPA allowed in 2024, 8th in 2025 and 7th now, so that part is real, not a five-game mirage. The offense was middle-of-the-pack the last two years. It has slid to 24th in EPA and 30th in yards per game, at 271 a game. Bo Nix is averaging about 188 passing yards a game, and the run game gets just 2.11 yards before contact.

The 3-2 record is built on margins. All three wins were one-score games, by 7, 4 and 6 points. The two losses came by 21 and 10. That leaves a -2.8 point differential per game and a net EPA that ranks 19th. A +0.6 turnover margin per game did a lot of work too: the defense took the ball away three times against the Chargers, who rank last in offensive EPA. Last year's 14-3 team went 0.846 in one-score games and won almost three games more than its point differential predicted. This franchise has been living on the close-game coin for a while, and coins don't stay loaded forever.

The pass defense is the strength, and it has a clear shape. It ranks 4th in deep-ball EPA allowed and 8th in explosive passes allowed, but 24th on short throws. It also has the league's worst missed-tackle rate, which is how the Rams threw for 390 yards in a game Denver still won. The run defense is a real hole, 28th in rush EPA allowed. The offense does have one quietly elite piece: the line allows the lowest QB hit rate in the league and a 3.4% sack rate. The passing game's problem is not protection. It is what happens once Nix has time.

Looking ahead, the remaining schedule is soft. Arizona, Miami, the winless Chargers and two Raiders games are all on it, so a winning record is very reachable. But this profile wins about 9 games, not 14. The immediate problem is that both starting corners, Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss, are out on a four-day turnaround. That cuts straight into the unit that makes this team work.

strengths.title: Pass defense that erases the deep ball
strengths.body: Denver ranks 3rd in pass EPA allowed and 4th in deep-pass EPA allowed. Opponents rarely get explosive shots, and it has been a multi-year trait, not a hot start. It does depend on the corners, though, and both starters are out this week.

strengths.title: Pass protection is genuinely elite
strengths.body: Nix is hit less often than any quarterback in the league, and the 3.4% sack rate ranks 4th. The four sacks in Week 1 at Kansas City look like the outlier: he has taken two sacks in the four games since. This should hold, and it gives the passing game a floor even while it is inefficient.

strengths.title: Getting home on the quarterback
strengths.body: The overall pressure rate is only 20th, but Denver converts: 5th in QB hit rate and 13 sacks, including five against the Chargers. When the rush arrives it finishes. That matters against offensive lines that leak.

concerns.title: Offense can't move the ball
concerns.body: The offense ranks 24th in EPA and 25th in success rate, and against the three top-six defenses it faced it scored 10, 20 and 14 points. Protection is fine, so the issue is creation. The run game gets little before contact, and the passing game has swung from -14.4 to +8.4 EPA week to week. With Pat Bryant on IR, the target tree narrows further, to Waddle, Sutton, Harvey and Engram.

concerns.title: Record outrunning the point differential
concerns.body: Denver is 3-0 in one-score games but has been outscored by 2.8 points a game. History says this franchise leans on close wins: last year it went 0.846 in one-score games and won 2.95 games over expected. Close-game results regress, and without them this is a .500 team.

concerns.title: Run defense and tackling leak
concerns.body: The run defense ranks 28th in rush EPA allowed and 24th in explosive runs, and Kansas City ran for 220 yards in Week 1. The league-worst missed-tackle rate is also why short passes (24th) turn into chunk gains. That is a structural flaw. With both starting corners out, more of the coverage burden falls on tackling after the catch.

trend.note: The passing EPA has whipsawed between -14.4 and +8.4 game to game with no clear direction. The defense has been the steady piece, peaking with five sacks and three takeaways against the league's worst offense in Week 5.

nextGame.headline: Two cornerbacks out, short week, and the league's second-best defense.
nextGame.body:
Seattle is the worst possible opponent for this offense. Its defense ranks 2nd in EPA, 2nd against the run, 3rd on third downs and 1st in yards allowed. Denver's below-average run game runs into a wall, and the deep shots are shut down too (Seattle is 3rd in deep EPA allowed). The soft spots are underneath: Seattle ranks 25th on short passes and 24th in EPA allowed to WR1s. That points to Waddle and to RJ Harvey out of the backfield, not to anything vertical. On the other side, Seattle's offense is nearly as bad as Denver's (26th in EPA), runs well below its expected pass rate despite a 30th-ranked run game, and gives up pressure at a bottom-seven rate. That is where Denver's pass rush can win the game.

Availability tilts toward Seattle. Denver has ruled out Pat Surtain II and Riley Moss, its two starting corners. Talanoa Hufanga, a 93% snap safety, did not practice Monday, so the back end could be badly thinned on a four-day turnaround. Seattle's main questions are Drew Lock (forearm, limited) and Jaxon Smith-Njigba (ankle, limited). If either sits, it would blunt the obvious plan of attacking Denver's depleted corners. A special-teams gap of more than six EPA a game also favors Seattle in what profiles as a low-scoring game.

keyMatchups.title: Denver rush vs Seattle's leaky line
keyMatchups.body: Denver's high QB hit rate meets a Seattle line that ranks 29th in QB hit rate allowed and 26th in pressure rate. Lock is limited with a forearm injury. If Denver gets home early, it can offset the missing corners by shortening the time they have to cover.

keyMatchups.title: Seattle's stubborn run game vs Denver
keyMatchups.body: Seattle runs more than expected even though its rushing EPA ranks 30th. Denver's run defense ranks 28th, so this is the one place a bad Seattle unit could find traction. Whichever weakness wins out shapes field position and the clock.

keyMatchups.title: Special teams field-position gap
keyMatchups.body: Seattle gains 5.07 EPA a game on special teams, 2nd in the league, while Denver loses 1.31. In a game totaled at 40.5 between two bottom-seven offenses, that gap could be the margin by itself.

nextGame.watch: Whether Drew Lock and Smith-Njigba play: a healthy Seattle passing game against Denver's backup corners is the most likely way this game breaks open.

restOfSeason.body:
The defense and the pass protection are sustainable; both have multi-season track records. The 3-0 mark in one-score games and the +0.6 turnover margin are not, and Denver should expect to split close games from here. The schedule is the saving grace. Arizona, Miami, the Chargers twice-ranked-last offense and a Raiders team near the middle offer winnable games, while Kansas City and Buffalo look like the clear losses. The corners' return estimates are short, so the pass defense should get back to its usual level soon.

The offense is the ceiling. Without a run game that creates on its own and with Bryant out until November, Denver will keep living around 19-20 points a game and winning with defense and the clock. That is a 9-win team in a division where Kansas City is already 4-0. A wild-card chase is realistic; a division title is not.
swingFactors: How quickly Surtain and Moss return
Regression in one-score games and turnovers
Whether the run game finds any yards before contact

bets.reason: Seattle has the better point differential (+5.8 vs -2.8 a game) and net EPA (0.043 vs -0.019). It also has a huge special-teams edge. Denver is missing both starting corners on a short week. The risk is Lock's forearm.

Two top-seven defenses face two bottom-seven offenses. Denver has gone under in four of five games, and its own offense has topped 20 points only once. The missing Denver corners are the main threat to the under.

Against top-six defenses Denver has scored 20, 14 and 23. Seattle allows the fewest yards in the league, ranks 2nd against the run and 3rd on third downs, and takes away the deep ball, which leaves Denver dinking against the 2nd-ranked defense.

confidence.note: Five games, but the defensive identity is backed by two prior seasons; the key cornerback injuries cloud the near term.
